name: Import a toolbox
intro: A module is reusable Python code grouped under a name. import makes a module available to your program. The standard library includes modules supplied with Python; no package installation is needed for these lessons.
prompt: Import math and print math.sqrt applied to any positive numeric literal.
why: You used import a toolbox in working Python.

name: Round up with ceil
intro: math.ceil returns the smallest integer that is not below a number. For a positive partial amount, it rounds upward. This helps when you need enough whole containers.
prompt: Import math, store a positive item count and a positive capacity, and print math.ceil(items / capacity) using your two variables.
hint:
import math
items = 7
capacity = 3
print(math.ceil(items / capacity))
why: You used round up with ceil in working Python.

name: Import one tool by name
intro: from module import tool brings one named tool into your program directly. Then call that tool without the module prefix. This is another import style, not another kind of function.
prompt: Use from math import sqrt, then print sqrt applied to a positive numeric literal without a math prefix.
why: You used import one tool by name in working Python.

name: Give a module a nickname
intro: as assigns an alias, a different local name for an imported module. The module itself does not change. A short alias can help when used clearly and consistently.
prompt: Import math with your own alias. Print the aliased module's sqrt of a positive numeric literal.
why: You used give a module a nickname in working Python.

name: Turn records into JSON text
intro: JSON is a text format for exchanging simple data. json.dumps converts a Python value such as your list of records into JSON text. This is called serialization: turning data into text that can be stored or passed on.
prompt: Import json, create at least two valid book records, convert the list with json.dumps, store the returned string and print it.
hint:
import json
books = [{"title": "Sky", "pages": 20}, {"title": "Sea", "pages": 30}]
text = json.dumps(books)
print(text)
why: You used turn records into json text in working Python.

name: Get records back from JSON
intro: json.loads reads JSON text and reconstructs the corresponding Python data. A list of records can make a round trip: Python list to JSON string and back to a Python list.
prompt: Import json. Make at least two book records, serialize them with dumps, decode that text with loads, and print the first restored record's title.
hint:
import json
books = [{"title": "Sky", "pages": 20}, {"title": "Sea", "pages": 30}]
text = json.dumps(books)
restored = json.loads(text)
print(restored[0]["title"])
why: You used get records back from json in working Python.
